title: 5.3 · Bits and pixels (How computers store things)
name: Bits and pixels (How computers store things)
summary: Students represent the same data several ways: binary and decimal, 0/1 pictures, gray levels from 0 to 255, RGB sliders to match a color swatch, and one color as a name, three numbers and a code. They work out how many colors a number of bits can show. Played in Inside the Machine's Bits & Pixels. One device per student.
iCan: represent the same data several ways: binary, decimal, pixels, gray levels and RGB
say how many values a number of bits can show
materials: binary cards (16 8 4 2 1), one set for the board
8 by 8 pixel grids (for the twin or the block day)
doNow: Send the word HI across the room with only a flashlight that turns on and off. How many flashes per letter?
plan: Explore: binary cards, then a color as three numbers

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 5.2, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 5.2

do: Give five students the binary cards 16 8 4 2 1; face up is on (1). Make the class's grade number, then write it in binary on the board.
Write 255, 0, 0 on the board and ask the question below. Then open Inside the Machine at Bits & Pixels on the projector (Open game at this chapter) and play level 1.
say: Everything in a computer is numbers, and every number is on/off switches.
The same data can be written many ways: a color name, three RGB numbers and a row of bits can all be the same color.
ask: Why does a color need three numbers?
explore.afterAsk: Take answers until someone says red, green and blue. Each number says how much of one light, from 0 to 255; 255, 0, 0 is pure red.
explore.bigIdea: The same data can be encoded many ways: binary, decimal, pixels and RGB.

play.solo: one device per student; a neighbor may read the numbers out loud, never touch your screen
lookFors: doubling wrong when reading binary: each card is twice the one to its right
moving all three RGB sliders together and getting only grays
play.misconception: Each extra bit does not add one more value: it doubles how many values you can show.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Why three numbers for a color?
How many colors can 2 bits show? How many with 3?
showMe: One student matches a swatch with the RGB sliders on the projector while the class calls out more red, less green.

exit.sentencePrompt: Pick one color or number from today and write it in two different ways.
exit.frame: ___ can be written as ___ or as ___.

rubric.line: Encoding: the same data in different forms
levels: Writes a number or a color in one form
Writes the same data correctly in two forms
Also says how many values a number of bits can show, or why a color needs three numbers

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: the binary cards on the board during Play
hint 1 sets one RGB slider for you
stretch: how many colors with 8 bits per pixel? Work it out by doubling

unpluggedTwin.title: Binary Cards and Pixel Grids
steps: Pairs convert five numbers between binary and decimal with the cards.
They color a pixel grid from rows of 0s and 1s, then recolor it with four gray levels using 2 bits per pixel.
They write the code for each gray level and count how many levels 3 bits would give.
Share: one picture, three encodings. Which takes the most bits?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: how could you send the word HI across the room with only a flashlight that turns on and off, and how many flashes per letter?

Play Inside the Machine, chapter Bits & Pixels, on your own for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 4 2 0 0. Goal: 4 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Why three numbers for a color?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut

add: the Binary Cards and Pixel Grids twin (15 minutes) before Play
10 minutes of the Unit 5 review on Brain Board

notes: Digits in game text are spaced, like 255 0 128, and RGB on the board is written 255, 0, 128.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: pixel, storage, gray level, decimal.
One device per student at this band.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Send the word HI across the room with only a flashlight that turns on and off. How many flashes per letter?

Big idea: The same data can be encoded many ways: binary, decimal, pixels and RGB.

We will talk about:
- Why three numbers for a color?
- How many colors can 2 bits show? How many with 3?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play: Bits & Pixels
steps.body:
Goal: 4 levels. Stretch: finish the chapter, then 3 stars.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 4 2 0 0.
One device each. A neighbor may help you think, but only you touch your screen.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about bits, colors and encoding.
